pos: n. (the largest English county, seat of the northern archbishopric and the ground on which the Pilgrimage of Grace was raised and sworn in 1536)
etymology: From York, Old English Eoforwic, itself from the Norse Jórvík and ultimately the British Eburacum; with scir, a shire or administrative division.
biblical_def: Yorkshire is the largest of the English counties, divided into three ridings, and it holds the northern archbishopric at York. Its great event in the Reformation is the Pilgrimage of Grace of 1536. When the lesser monasteries were suppressed, the north rose; Robert Aske, a Yorkshire lawyer, took the leadership of a host that marched under a banner of the Five Wounds and bound its members by an oath to restore the houses and remove the king's evil counsellors. They took York and Pontefract and faced the Duke of Norfolk at Doncaster, where they accepted a pardon and a promise of a parliament; the promise was broken, a fresh disturbance gave the pretext, and Aske was hanged at York in 1537 with some two hundred others. The county afterward went two ways: the North and East Ridings kept a strong recusant gentry well into the seventeenth century, while the clothing towns of the West Riding became as Puritan as any district in England and furnished a long line of preachers and, after 1662, of ejected ministers. The dictionary records the oath as the heart of the matter, and holds that a vow made to God binds and a vow made to bind God's church to an error does not excuse the swearer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vow as a solemn promise made to God; a pilgrimage as a journey to a sacred place; to swear as to affirm with an appeal to God; a riding as one of the three divisions of Yorkshire; and a recusant as one who refuses to conform.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn promise to perform some act.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion at a shrine.
SWEAR, v.i. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
RIDING, n. One of the three divisions or jurisdictions of the county of York in England.
RECUSANT, n. One who refuses communion with the church of England; a nonconformist, particularly a Roman Catholic.
scriptures: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.
Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared.
corruption_summary: Largest English county and seat of the northern archbishopric, where Robert Aske raised and swore the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536 and was hanged at York the following year.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the sworn confederacy, a body of men binding themselves by oath to a religious programme and treating the oath thereafter as a higher obligation than the truth of the thing sworn. The Pilgrims of Grace took such an oath, and it held them when a prudent man would have gone home. Scripture takes vows with the utmost seriousness and for that very reason will not let a man shelter behind one: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecc 5:4) stands beside the warning that the LORD has no pleasure in fools, and a man who swears to restore a false worship has sworn foolishly and is not thereby obliged to do it. The psalmist's rule is simple and it assumes the object is right: “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God” (Psa 76:11).

The second paragraph names the lawful pattern, which the risings travestied. Scripture does know of a people covenanting together in a public act, and both its great instances are reformations and not rebellions. Josiah stood by a pillar and “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ki 23:3), and the people stood to it; Joshua set the choice before Israel and answered for his own household, “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). In both the covenant is to obey what God has already commanded, not to compel a king. The Yorkshire oath of 1536 was sworn to restore suppressed houses, and the dictionary holds that this reverses the pattern: men bound themselves to defend what Scripture had not established, and they paid for it at York.

Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, the thing promised; “pay that which thou hast vowed”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be complete, to pay, to make good; “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God”, Psalm 76:11.
Hebrew kesil (H3684) — a fool, a dull or stubborn man; “he hath no pleasure in fools”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.

“made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD” (2Ki 23:3) — the lawful pattern the rising reversed.
“but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15) — the West Riding clothing towns after 1662.

pos: n. (the north-western English county that remained the most recusant in the kingdom and at the same time bred the strongest northern Puritanism)
etymology: From Lancaster, the Roman camp on the Lune, from the river name and Old English ceaster, a fortified town; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Lancashire is the county between the Mersey and the Lune, and it is the sharpest division in English religious geography. Through the whole of Elizabeth's reign and long after, its gentry held to Rome in greater numbers than anywhere else in England; the Commission for Causes Ecclesiastical reported whole hundreds where the old service was kept in private houses, seminary priests moved between the halls of the Catholic families, and the recusancy fines fell on the same names for generations. Yet the same county produced the most vigorous Puritanism in the north. Bolton was called the Geneva of the north; Manchester's collegiate church had a succession of preaching wardens; Richard Mather of Lowton, Henry Newcome of Manchester and the Lancashire classis of the sixteen-forties made the county a stronghold of Presbyterian order, and the Lancashire ministers subscribed a harmonious consent to the Westminster standards. After 1662 its dissent was numerous and stubborn. The dictionary records the county as a place where two religions lived side by side in one shire for a century and a half, and it names the duty that arises in such a place, which is doctrinal separation without personal malice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a recusant as one who refuses conformity; a heretic as one who holds an error in the fundamentals of religion; to withdraw as to retire or take back; a classis as an assembly of elders; and separation as the act of parting.
webster_full: RECUSANT, n. One who refuses communion with the church of England; a nonconformist; particularly a Roman Catholic.
HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the Christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
WITHDRAW, v.t. To take back; to recall; to retire; to retreat from a place or from company.
CLASSIS, n. An assembly or body of ministers and elders exercising jurisdiction over several churches.
SEPARATION, n. The act of separating; disjunction; the state of being apart or divided.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.
If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:
corruption_summary: North-western county that held more recusant gentry than any other in England while breeding the strongest northern Puritanism, with Bolton called the Geneva of the north.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the gospel of Rome, and the dictionary names it as another gospel rather than as a variant of the same one, because that is the only category Paul leaves available. A religion of the mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, of merit, of a treasury of satisfactions and of a priesthood interposed between a man and his Mediator is not a different emphasis within the faith but a substitution for it, and the apostolic sentence is passed without qualification: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). Lancashire's Protestant ministers were not uncharitable for holding this; they were holding what Galatians says.

The second paragraph is about conduct, because a county where the two religions were neighbours put the question practically, and the dictionary answers it from the texts that govern it rather than from sentiment. Separation is commanded and it is ecclesiastical: an obstinate man is to be refused after due admonition, for “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10); the disorderly brother is to be withdrawn from, since Paul commands “that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly” (2Th 3:6); and the teacher of a false Christ is not to be received as a teacher, for if a man “bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed” (2Jn 1:10). None of this licenses informing, fining or dispossessing a neighbour, and the recusancy statutes did all three. The dictionary holds the doctrine and refuses the apparatus of persecution that Protestant Lancashire used to enforce it.

“A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10) — separation as ecclesiastical, not civil.
“receive him not into your house” (2Jn 1:10) — the seminary priests moving between houses.

pos: n. (the northernmost English county, holding Lindisfarne and Jarrow, from which the Gospel went out to the English and the Continent)
etymology: Old English Norþhymbraland, the land of those dwelling north of the Humber.
biblical_def: Northumberland is the northernmost English county, running from the Tyne to the Tweed, and in the seventh and eighth centuries it was the brightest spot in western Christendom. Aidan came from Iona at the invitation of King Oswald in 635 and settled on the tidal island of Lindisfarne, and from there the northern English were converted by preachers who went on foot; Cuthbert was bishop there and became the great northern saint; the Lindisfarne Gospels were written and illuminated in that house about 700. At Wearmouth and Jarrow, Benedict Biscop built libraries out of books bought in Rome, and Bede wrote in them, producing the Ecclesiastical History and a mass of commentary, and translating the Gospel of John into English on his deathbed in 735. From this county Willibrord and later Boniface's circle went to the Frisians and the Germans, and Alcuin went from York to Charlemagne. The Danes sacked Lindisfarne in 793 and the age ended. The dictionary records the learning and the mission with gratitude, names the cult of Cuthbert's body and the traffic in his relics as the corruption that grew out of the gift, and marks the county as a standing proof that a dark place is lit from without.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a monastery as a house of religious retirement; a scriptorium's root, to transcribe, as to copy; illumination as the act of enlightening; relics as the remains of a saint; and a missionary as one sent to propagate religion.
webster_full: MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from the world, for persons devoted to religion.
TRANSCRIBE, v.t. To copy; to write over again, or in the same words; to write a copy of anything.
ILLUMINATION, n. The act of illuminating; that which gives light; the adorning of a book with colours and gold.
RELICS, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to him, preserved and venerated.
MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent to preach the gospel in a foreign land.
scriptures: Isa 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
Joh 1:5
And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
corruption_summary: Northernmost English county holding Lindisfarne and Jarrow, converted from Iona by Aidan in 635 and the seat of Bede's learning, until the Danes sacked the island in 793.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that grew here grew out of a genuine gift, and the dictionary separates the two carefully. Cuthbert was a true preacher and a holy man; what was made of him afterward was a cult. His body was treated as incorrupt and carried about the north for generations as a possession, his shrine at Durham drew offerings and privileges, and the monks of the house built their wealth and their legal claims upon the dead man's bones. That is the traffic in relics in its clearest English form, and Scripture knows nothing of it: the apostolic commission is “To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18), and a reliquary opens nobody's eyes. The dictionary honours Cuthbert by declining to venerate him.

The second paragraph states what the county proves, and it is a doctrine rather than a sentiment. Northumbria did not grow its own light. Aidan came over from Iona because a king asked for a preacher; the books at Jarrow were bought abroad and carried home; the mission that went out to Frisia and Germany was a debt being repaid. Isaiah describes the whole transaction as something done to a people rather than by them, for “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2), and John insists that the light is not generated by the darkness it enters, since “the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not” (Joh 1:5). Paul grounds the whole work in a creative act, naming “God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness” (2Co 4:6) as the one who has shined in human hearts. A county that was evangelised by a man walking down from Iona has no ground for boasting and every ground for sending.

“the darkness comprehended it not” (Joh 1:5) — the Danish sack of Lindisfarne, 793.
“from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18) — what a reliquary cannot do.

pos: n. (the north-western border county of Carlisle and the fells, long a lawless march and from 1652 a cradle of the Quaker movement)
etymology: From the Brittonic Cymry, fellow-countrymen, preserved in the name of the British kingdom of Cumbria; with Old English land.
biblical_def: Cumberland is the north-western border county, running from the Solway and Carlisle up into the high fells, and until the union of the crowns it was one of the lawless marches. The Debatable Land lay along its northern edge, and the reiving families on both sides of the line raided, blackmailed and burned for generations while the wardens of the marches failed to govern them; the parish churches were poor and often unserved, and whole valleys went for years without preaching. Out of that neglect came an unusual receptiveness. The Seekers of the north-west, scattered companies who had abandoned the parish worship as unlawful and waited without ordinances for a further light, were numerous here, and when George Fox came north in 1652 he gathered them; Pardshaw Crag and the valleys west of Keswick became Quaker ground, and Cumberland sent out many of the movement's first travelling preachers. The dictionary records the vacancy before it records the harvest, and holds that where no watchman is set the ground does not stay empty but is taken by whatever comes. A county may be lost by what its ministers failed to say as surely as by what its raiders did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a march as the frontier of a country; a reiver's root, to reave, as to take away by violence; a breach as a gap; a watchman as one set to guard; and a foundation as the basis of a structure.
webster_full: MARCH, n. A border; a frontier; the confine or limit of a territory, as the marches of Scotland.
REAVE, v.t. To take away by violence; to bereave; to rob or plunder.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking, as a breach in a wall.
WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch or keep guard over a city or a flock.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that upon which anything stands and is supported.
scriptures: And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Lam 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
corruption_summary: North-western border county of Carlisle and the fells, long a lawless march with unserved parishes, where the Seekers were numerous and George Fox gathered them from 1652.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is ours and it is a negative one: the vacancy of a pastorate. Cumberland's livings were poor, its parishes enormous and its moorland chapels often served by a reading minister or by nobody, and a church that leaves a county in that state for a century has no answer to make when another body gathers it. Ezekiel puts the want in exactly these terms, as a search for a man that failed: “And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none” (Eze 22:30). The psalmist asks the consequent question and the dictionary does not pretend it has an easy answer: “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3).

The second paragraph names the error that filled the gap, because the dictionary will not treat the Quaker gathering as a simple mercy. The Seekers had concluded that no true church, ministry or ordinance remained on earth, and waited for an immediate light; Fox confirmed them in it. The Reformed answer is that Christ has not left His church without Word, baptism or supper, and that the man who abandons the ordinances because the ministers are bad has mistaken a famine for an abolition. Jeremiah's picture of a people whose “prophets also find no vision from the LORD” (Lam 2:9) is a description of judgment, not a programme for worship. And the duty laid on men in a disordered place is not withdrawal but intercession and labour where they are, for the command to the captives was to “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7).

Hebrew gadar (H1443) — to wall in or up, to repair a hedge; “that should make up the hedge”, Ezekiel 22:30.

“her prophets also find no vision from the LORD” (Lam 2:9) — the Seekers abandoning the ordinances.
“seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7) — the duty of men in a disordered place.

pos: n. (the small northern county of the high fells where the Westmorland Seekers were gathered at Firbank Fell in 1652)
etymology: Old English Westmoringaland, the land of the people of the western moors.
biblical_def: Westmorland is the small northern county of high fell and narrow dale lying between Lancashire and Cumberland, with Appleby as its county town and Kendal as its market. Its churches were few and its dales remote, and in the sixteen-forties several companies of what were called Seekers formed there, meeting at Preston Patrick and elsewhere under men like Francis Howgill and John Audland; they had left the parish assemblies, held that the true ministry had failed, and met in silence to wait. In June 1652 George Fox, coming over from Pendle, preached on Firbank Fell to a large gathering of these companies for some three hours, and most of them were convinced; Westmorland and the neighbouring dales furnished a large part of the band of travelling preachers who carried Quakerism through England and overseas. The dictionary records the event because it is the clearest English case of a vacancy in teaching being filled by an error, and it records the Seekers' question honestly: they were right that much preaching in their dales was dead, and wrong in the conclusion they drew. Searching is commanded; the standard searched by is the Scriptures.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seeker as one who seeks, applied to a sect waiting for a new revelation; to search as to look over with care; counsel as advice or deliberation; a dale as a valley; and silence as the state of holding the peace.
webster_full: SEEKER, n. One that seeks; applied to persons who profess no determinate religion, but wait for a further revelation.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to examine with care.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request; deliberation; consultation.
DALE, n. A vale or valley; a low place between hills.
SILENCE, n. Stillness; the state of a place where no sound is uttered; forbearance of speech.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
corruption_summary: Small northern county of high fells where companies of Seekers met in silence at Preston Patrick until George Fox preached on Firbank Fell in June 1652 and convinced most of them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Seeker position itself, which the dictionary states fairly before rejecting it: that the apostolic ministry, the church and the ordinances had all failed and perished, so that a believer's duty was to wait in silence for an immediate illumination. The error is not the dissatisfaction; it is the conclusion. The Bereans are commended for a procedure that keeps both halves together, receiving the word readily and then testing it, for they “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). A company that has given up the Scriptures as its standard has no way of telling a light from a fancy, and the Quaker doctrine of the inner light removed the only instrument by which Fox's own preaching could have been tested.

The second paragraph grants what ought to be granted. The dales were badly taught, and the Seekers' hunger was real; God does guide, and He does so by a word, for “thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it” (Isa 30:21), which is instruction and not impression. The sovereignty of the Spirit in conversion is not in doubt either, since “The wind bloweth where it listeth” (Joh 3:8); but a sovereign Spirit who works freely is not therefore a Spirit who works without means. The remedy Malachi records for a generation whose public religion had gone cold is neither silence nor a new revelation but believers speaking to each other under God's hearing, for “they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it” (Mal 3:16). Conference about the Word, and not waiting without it, is the road out of a dead parish.

“spake often one to another” (Mal 3:16) — the road out of a dead parish.

pos: n. (the Yorkshire minster town whose Saxon crypt was built by Wilfrid about 672 and which was a collegiate church of canons until the Dissolution)
etymology: Old English Hrýpum, at the Hrype, the dative plural of a tribal name; the Latin form is Ripon.
biblical_def: Ripon is the Yorkshire town on the Ure whose minster stands over a Saxon crypt built by Wilfrid about 672, one of the oldest pieces of masonry in England still in use. Wilfrid founded a Benedictine house here and built his church of dressed stone with masons brought from Gaul, and the crypt survived every later rebuilding above it. The Danes destroyed the monastery; the church was refounded as a collegiate establishment of secular canons, which it remained until the Dissolution took its college away in 1547, after which it served simply as a very large parish church until it was made a cathedral in 1836. Its liturgical peculiarity was the Use of York rather than Sarum. The dictionary's interest is in what a collegiate church was for: a body of canons endowed to maintain the daily office in choir, which is to say a foundation whose purpose was the recitation of services rather than the preaching of the Word to a congregation. When the college went, the preaching remained to be supplied. The dictionary holds that a building is justified by the worship done in it, and that reading and exhortation, not ceremony, are the substance of that worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crypt as a subterranean cell or chapel; a canon as a cathedral dignitary; collegiate as pertaining to a college; the office as the daily service; and to expound as to explain or lay open.
webster_full: CRYPT, n. A subterranean cell or cave, especially under a church, for the interment of the dead.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral.
COLLEGIATE, a. Pertaining to a college; containing a college, as a collegiate church.
OFFICE, n. That which a person does in an official capacity; the daily service of the church; a formulary of devotion.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.

Luk 4:16
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
And after the reading of the law and the prophets the rulers of the synagogue sent unto them, saying, Ye men and brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: Yorkshire minster town whose Saxon crypt Wilfrid built about 672, a collegiate church of canons endowed for the daily office until the Dissolution took its college in 1547.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is the collegiate foundation itself as an institution, and the dictionary names it carefully because the men who staffed it were not necessarily bad men. A college of canons was endowed so that services might be sung in choir in perpetuity, and the endowment attached the revenue to the recitation rather than to the teaching of a people. That is a misallocation at the root, and it produced the thing the Reformation found everywhere: splendid buildings with daily offices and parishes without sermons. The psalmist's preference is for presence in God's house rather than office in it, choosing to “be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10), and a prebend is not what he had in mind.

The second paragraph sets out the pattern the dictionary holds to, and it is a synagogue pattern rather than a choir pattern. Our Lord's own custom in the place where He was brought up was to go in and read, for “as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read” (Luk 4:16); and at Antioch the order of service was reading followed by exhortation, the rulers asking “if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on” (Act 13:15). Reading and exposition, in that order, are the substance. What they accomplish is stated plainly, and it is the opposite of mystification: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). A crypt that has stood since 672 is a remarkable thing, and the dictionary values it; but the church above it was worth more after 1547 than before, because the people in it were taught.

pos: n. (the East Riding minster town whose sanctuary and frith stool gave refuge to fugitives and whose shrine of John of Beverley drew northern pilgrims)
etymology: Old English Beoferlic, the beaver clearing or beaver lodge, from beofor, a beaver, and a word for a clearing or stream.
biblical_def: Beverley is the market town of the East Riding of Yorkshire, dominated by a minster larger than many cathedrals. It grew round the monastery founded by John of Beverley, bishop of York, who died there in 721 and whose shrine became one of the chief objects of northern pilgrimage; Beverley was the third richest cult centre in the north after Durham and York. The minster held a right of sanctuary with a defined area marked by crosses on the roads out of the town, and inside the church stood the frith stool, a plain stone seat on which a fugitive sat to claim the peace of the church; the sanctuary registers survive and list hundreds of men who came in, many of them killers, and who were then given a term to compound or to leave the realm. The shrine was destroyed and the sanctuary abolished at the Reformation. The dictionary records the sanctuary with a divided verdict: the instinct that a hunted man should have somewhere to go is biblical, and the apparatus that grew round the bones of a bishop is not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sanctuary as a sacred place and a place of protection; a refuge as a shelter from danger; a fugitive as one who flees; a shrine as a case for sacred relics; and to compound as to settle a matter by agreement.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; a place of protection; a sacred asylum, where criminals took refuge from punishment.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
FUGITIVE, n. One who flees from his station or duty; one who flees from danger or from justice.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; the tomb of a saint, resorted to by devotees.
COMPOUND, v.t. To settle by agreement or composition; to discharge a debt by paying a part.
scriptures: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Rev 3:2
Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die: for I have not found thy works perfect before God.
Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
corruption_summary: East Riding minster town whose frith stool and marked sanctuary gave refuge to hundreds of fugitives, and whose shrine of John of Beverley was the third richest cult centre in the north.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the shrine and not the sanctuary. A bishop who died in 721 was made the proprietor of a town's prosperity: offerings came in, privileges were granted on his account, the relics were carried in procession in time of trouble, and the minster's wealth was built on the traffic. The dictionary names this as the cult of the saints, with its invocation, its merit and its reliquary, and holds that it displaces the one Mediator and the one atonement. The city the believer is actually directed to look for is not built over anybody's bones, for Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10).

The second paragraph grants what should be granted and then presses the harder point. The frith stool answered to a real and biblical instinct, since the law of Israel appointed cities to which a man who had killed without malice might flee; and the abolition of sanctuary left England with no equivalent provision at all, which is not obviously an improvement. But a town that lived off a shrine and then lost it faced the question the risen Christ puts to churches that have declined from a former state: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5). The remedy is not nostalgia for the pilgrim trade but the strengthening of what is left, for the word to Sardis is “Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die” (Rev 3:2). And the warning proper to a place that had great religious advantage and little fruit from it is the warning to the favoured towns of Galilee, “Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida!” (Mat 11:21).

pos: n. (the north Yorkshire abbey on the cliff where the synod of 664 settled the Easter question for the English church)
etymology: Old Norse Hvítabýr, the white settlement; the earlier English name was Streanaeshalch.
biblical_def: Whitby is the north Yorkshire port under the cliff on which Hild founded a double monastery of men and women in 657. Caedmon, a herdsman of that house, made the first Christian verse in English there. In 664 King Oswiu called a synod at Whitby to settle a dispute that had divided his own household: the Irish and Iona tradition, brought to Northumbria by Aidan, kept Easter by one reckoning, and the Roman tradition by another, and the two usages ran side by side in one kingdom so that the king and queen kept the feast on different days. Colman spoke for Iona on the authority of Columba, Wilfrid for Rome on the authority of Peter, and Oswiu decided for the Roman reckoning; Colman withdrew to Iona with those who would not conform. The dictionary records the synod as a genuine council rightly held and wrongly argued. A church may and should meet to settle a disputed question, and a calendar question is a lawful matter for such a meeting; but the ground on which it was decided was the prestige of a see, and that ground is not available.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; a schism as a division in a church; order as regular disposition; unity as the state of being one; and usage as long-continued practice.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastical persons to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of elders.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; particularly, a division in a church, on account of difference of opinion.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; settled mode of proceeding.
UNITY, n. The state of being one; concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
USAGE, n. Long-continued practice; customary manner of acting; custom; habitual use.
scriptures: Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: North Yorkshire abbey founded by Hild in 657, where the synod of 664 settled the Easter reckoning for the English church on the authority of the see of Peter.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the argument, not the assembly. Wilfrid carried the day at Whitby by urging the authority of Peter and of the see that claimed him, and Oswiu decided accordingly; that reasoning, developed over the following centuries, became the papal claim itself, and the dictionary names it as the root corruption of western church government. A council is to be decided by Scripture. The Jerusalem assembly is the pattern and it reasoned from the written word and from God's own attested acts, the brethren determining that the question should go “up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2) and then settling it by argument rather than by precedence. A synod that decides by prestige has not deliberated; it has deferred.

The second paragraph defends the synod against the opposite error, which is the modern dislike of councils altogether. The dictionary holds that assemblies of elders are lawful, useful and commanded in their place. Solomon states the principle, that “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22); Paul closes a chapter on disordered worship with the standing rule, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40); and the duty of men on both sides of such a dispute is stated as an active labour, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). Two Easters in one royal household was a real disorder and it was right to end it. Colman's withdrawal to Iona was the act of a man who would not be ruled by Rome, and the dictionary, which also will not be, honours him for it while allowing that he lost the argument he actually made.

pos: n. (the Northumberland abbey town whose Saxon crypt Wilfrid built about 674 out of dressed Roman stone taken from Corbridge)
etymology: Old English Hagustaldes ham, the homestead of a hagustald, a younger son holding land outside the family holding.
biblical_def: Hexham is the Northumberland market town on the Tyne, where Wilfrid founded a monastery about 674 on land given him by Queen Etheldreda and built a church which Eddius said had no equal north of the Alps. Its crypt survives, and it is built of dressed stone carried from the ruined Roman town and bridge at Corbridge a few miles downriver; some of the blocks still carry Roman inscriptions and dedications to Roman gods, turned inward or set as rubble in the walls of a Christian church. Hexham was briefly a bishopric; the Danes destroyed the monastery, and it was refounded as an Augustinian priory which survived until the Dissolution and whose church became the parish church. The frith stool in the chancel is Saxon work, possibly Wilfrid's own bishop's seat. In 1464 the Lancastrians were destroyed near the town. The dictionary records the crypt as an emblem worth keeping: the stones of a dead religion, dressed by other hands for other altars, carried off and built into the foundations of a house where God was to be praised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crypt as a subterranean chapel; spoil as that taken from an enemy; to repair as to restore after decay; a foundation as the basis of a building; and to consecrate as to set apart for sacred use.
webster_full: CRYPT, n. A subterranean cell or cave, especially under a church, used for burial or for a chapel.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; the slough or cast skin of a serpent.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, waste or injury; to mend; to refit.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the basis or ground-work.
CONSECRATE, v.t. To make or declare to be sacred, by certain ceremonies; to devote to the service of God.
scriptures: Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
corruption_summary: Northumberland abbey town whose surviving Saxon crypt Wilfrid built about 674 from dressed Roman stone taken from Corbridge, some blocks still carrying dedications to Roman gods.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the material of a false religion may be put to honest use, while its forms may not. The masons who built Wilfrid's crypt carried off the dressed blocks of a Roman town, inscriptions and all, and laid them in a Christian foundation; the stone was good and the gods it had been cut for were nothing, so the stone was used. That is the right instinct, and Isaiah gives the figure of it in the beating of weapons into tools, when “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks” (Isa 2:4). What may not be carried over is the worship. The rule on that is absolute and it closes the door on borrowing rites as cleanly as it opens the door on borrowing stone: “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).

The second thing to recover is the scale on which God works and the duty of recording it. Hexham is a small town and its crypt is a low, cramped, dark room, and it has outlasted the empire whose stones it is made of and the monastery that was built above it. Zechariah rebukes the instinct to despise such beginnings, asking “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10) of a temple being rebuilt by a remnant. And where a thing has in fact been done, the duty of a generation is to tell the next one, for “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done” (Psa 78:4). A crypt is a tolerable way of telling it, so long as nobody begins to pray in it to the men who built it.

pos: n. (the Westmorland wool town of Kendal Green cloth, an early centre of northern dissent and of the Quaker movement after 1652)
etymology: From Kirkby Kendal, the church town in the dale of the Kent, from the river name and Old Norse dalr, a valley.
biblical_def: Kendal is the market and manufacturing town of Westmorland, standing in the valley of the Kent, and for centuries the wool town of the northern fells. Flemish weavers were settled there in the fourteenth century, and the coarse green woollen cloth called Kendal Green was carried all over England; the town's motto, wool is my bread, states the case exactly. The trade gave the place a population of independent artisans rather than tenants, which is the usual soil of dissent, and so it proved. Kendal was a centre of the Westmorland Seekers in the sixteen-forties, and after Fox's preaching on Firbank Fell in 1652 it became one of the earliest and largest Quaker meetings in England, with a meeting house and a burial ground and a steady stream of sufferings recorded under the Quaker Act and the Conventicle Acts; the merchant families of the town paid the fines and kept the meeting. The dictionary records Kendal as a town whose religion grew out of its looms, and takes the occasion to set out the husbandman's virtue, which is patience, and the shepherd's duty, which is to know the state of his flock.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a husbandman as a farmer or tiller of the ground; a flock as a company of sheep; patience as the suffering of afflictions with calmness; a pasture as ground for grazing; and a fleece as the coat of wool shorn from a sheep.
webster_full: HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labours in tillage.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper.
PASTURE, n. Grass for the food of cattle; the food of cattle taken by grazing; ground covered with grass.
FLEECE, n. The coat of wool that covers a sheep, or that is shorn from a sheep at one time.
scriptures: Jam 5:7

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing.
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: Westmorland wool town of Kendal Green cloth whose independent artisans made it a Seeker centre in the sixteen-forties and one of the earliest large Quaker meetings in England after 1652.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one a wool town is well placed to learn, that the work God sets men is slow and that the virtue proper to it is patience rather than contrivance. James sends his readers to the farmer for the lesson, since “the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain” (Jam 5:7); a fleece cannot be hurried and neither can a harvest. The dales around Kendal lived by that fact, and the psalmist's picture of a countryside doing what it was made to do is a fair description of them: “The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn” (Psa 65:13).

The second thing to recover is the transfer of the figure, which Scripture makes constantly and which a sheep country ought to find easy. The charge to know one's flock is given first about animals and is meant to be carried over, for “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23) is addressed to a man with a pastorate of some kind whether he keeps sheep or people. And the measure of the office is set by the one who holds it perfectly: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11). The Kendal Quakers kept their meeting through fines and distraints, and their merchants paid for it out of the cloth trade; the dictionary dissents from their doctrine of the inner light and records their steadiness under the law as a rebuke to churches that have lost neither doctrine nor liberty and keep nothing.
